newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: INP says has no intention to up W&H bid.
newsitem.headline: INP says has no intention to up W&H bid.

text.p: Independent Newspapers Plc on Thursday said it had no intention of raising its NZ$11.00/share bid for New Zealand publisher Wilson and Horton and would be happy with less than 100 percent of the company.
"There is absolutely no intention at this point in time to raise the bid," INP Finance Director James Parkinson told Reuters in an interview.
But Parkinson qualified his statement, saying "you would never say never".

"I would never rule out categorically any raising (of the bid) because one always goes back and looks to see what has happened and see if there are changed circumstances, but I see absolutely no reason why we would at this point in time."
He said INP would happily accept less than 100 percent control of Wilson and Horton because its main aim was to consolidate the publisher.

"We're offering to buy 100 percent (of Wilson and Horton), but it's not essential. What we really want to do is be able to consolidate. We want to take the holding on board and we want to have effective control," he said.

"Under consolidation, you take in 100 percent of the assets, you take in 100 percent of the operating profit and the cash flow, and then to the extent that you don't own 100 percent, you then allocate to minority interests."
Asked if INP would be satisfied with, for example, only 70 percent control of Wilson and Horton, Parkinson replied: "Yes, absolutely."

However, he said INP was very happy with the way the bid was progressing, particularly acceptances of the exchangeable share option, which gave investors the opportunity to continue their participation in Wilson and Horton.
He said the offer of 1.375 exchangeable INP shares for each Wilson and Horton share had become more attractive since it was first made because INP's share price had risen.

Independent Press Communications Ltd, the INP subsidiary making the bid, said earlier it had picked up 18.14 percent of W&H shares on top of the 45.15 percent originally held by INP and family trusts linked to principal Tony O'Reilly.

Parkinson said that once INP had taken control of Wilson and Horton, it would look to restructure New Zealand's largest circulation newspaper, the New Zealand Herald, and could consider raising its cover price.

"I think one would look at some restructuring, yes, but restructuring in the sense of improving the product. There are various ways that one could look at improving it, particularly I think in the business section, and as a result generate increased revenue," he said.
"Possibly one's got to look then at cover prices. If you have a much better product, then you get a better price for that better product."
He said it was impossible to say whether INP would look to divest itself of smaller entities within the Wilson and Horton group that were not profitable.

"We would tend to be very much focused towards revenue enhancement than rationalisation, but we'd have to have a look and make a decision. At this point in time I think we would feel that there is scope for revenue enhancement and therefore hopefully increased profitability."

He said after Wilson and Horton had been consolidated, New Zealand would contribute the largest portion of INP's operating profit -- 40.6 percent, which compared with 31.3 percent from Ireland and 19.8 percent from South Africa.
New Zealand would also contribute 33.3 percent of the group's revenue. -- Wellington Newsroom (64 4) 4734746
